questions.q: Describe the main features of the political structure of the Roman Empire.
answer: The Roman Empire rested on three main pillars: the emperor, the Senate and the army.

answer.text: The emperor was the supreme authority, controlling the government, the army and the law. Augustus established this system, the Principate, after the fall of the Republic, though in theory he ruled with the goodwill of the Senate.

The Senate was a body of the wealthy aristocracy that had governed during the Republic and continued to enjoy great prestige. A good emperor was expected to respect the Senate, while those who ignored it were remembered as tyrants.
The Roman army was a paid, professional force of volunteers. Because it could make or unmake emperors, it was a decisive political factor, and its support was essential for any ruler.

answer: The balance between these three shaped the stability of the empire.

questions.q: What major religious and cultural changes marked the period of Late Antiquity in the Roman world?
answer: Late Antiquity, roughly the fourth to the seventh centuries, was a time of deep religious and cultural transformation in the Roman world.

answer.text: Christianity, once a persecuted faith, spread widely and gained official favour under the emperor Constantine, who converted in the fourth century. It soon became the state religion of the empire, changing its cultural and moral outlook.

The empire was reorganised, with a new capital at Constantinople in the east, and the eastern, or Byzantine, half grew stronger while the west weakened. New art, architecture and ways of thought developed.
In the seventh century the rise of Islam in Arabia and its rapid expansion reshaped the whole region.

answer: These changes ended the classical world and opened the medieval age.
